client: I just got my final project grade back, and it was way lower than I expected. I worked so hard on it, and now I can't stop thinking that maybe I'm just not cut out for this program. I know you're supposed to help with stuff like this, but I'm not sure talking about it will change the fact that I might not be good enough.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling really disappointed and doubting yourself after receiving this grade, especially after putting in so much effort. When we're in this headspace, our minds often jump to the worst conclusions—what makes you think this one grade means you're not cut out for the program?

client: Because it's not just this one grade - I've been barely scraping by in most of my classes. This was the project I actually felt good about, and now even that turned out bad. Maybe I'm just not as smart as everyone else here, and I'm fooling myself by staying in this program. I don't see how thinking differently about it will magically make me do better.
therapist: You're carrying a heavy weight of discouragement after seeing this pattern in your grades, and it makes sense you'd question your place in the program. When you say "I'm not as smart as everyone else," what evidence do you have for that thought—and what evidence might not fit that story?

client: I guess the evidence is that I'm struggling while others seem to get it so easily. But...I did get accepted into this program, so someone must have thought I could do it. It's just hard to believe that when I keep seeing bad grades. I don't know how that helps me though - knowing I got in doesn't make the work any easier now.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between recognizing that you were accepted into the program for a reason and feeling overwhelmed by the challenges you're facing now. What would it look like to focus on small, manageable steps to improve, rather than comparing yourself to others or judging your overall ability?

client: Small steps sound nice in theory, but I don't even know where to start. Every time I try to study or work on assignments, I get overwhelmed thinking about how far behind I am. It feels like no matter what small step I take, it won't be enough to catch up with everyone else.
therapist: The weight of feeling behind can make even small steps feel impossible right now—that sense of overwhelm is completely understandable. What if we focused first on just one assignment or concept, without comparing it to where others are? Where might you begin if you gave yourself permission to go at your own pace?

client: I guess I could start with the material I struggled with most on this last project. But part of me thinks "what's the point?" because even when I focus on one thing, I still make mistakes. It feels like I'm just delaying the inevitable realization that maybe this program is too hard for me.
therapist: I hear how defeated you're feeling—like every effort leads back to the same discouraging place. But I notice something important: even in this heaviness, you're still able to identify where to begin ("the material I struggled with most"). What would it feel like to approach just that one area with curiosity rather than judgment, as an experiment rather than a test of your worth?

client: I've never really thought about learning that way before. I guess I always see everything as a test of whether I'm good enough. But the idea of just exploring one concept without that pressure... it sounds nice, but I'm not sure I can actually do it. My mind automatically goes to "you have to get this right" mode.
therapist: I can hear the shift in your voice as you consider this new approach—there's a mix of cautious hope and understandable skepticism. That "get it right" mode is so automatic for you—what would happen if, just for one study session, you treated mistakes not as proof you're not good enough, but as valuable information about where to focus next?

client: I can try to think that way, but my stomach still clenches at the thought of looking at my mistakes. What if I try seeing them as learning opportunities and still don't improve? That might feel even worse, like I'm failing at this new approach too. It's scary to hope things could be different.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling both a glimmer of possibility and some understandable fear about trying this new approach—your mind is already anticipating how it might go wrong. That tension between hope and fear is completely normal when we try something unfamiliar. What would it feel like to start small—maybe just 15 minutes of approaching one concept with curiosity—rather than expecting yourself to completely shift how you view mistakes all at once?

client: 15 minutes sounds manageable, but I'm worried it won't be enough to make a difference. What if I try it and still feel just as lost? Part of me thinks I should be spending hours studying, not just 15 minutes—otherwise I'll fall even further behind. It's hard to balance trying something new with the pressure to catch up.
therapist: I hear you caught between wanting to try this new approach and feeling the persistent pressure to make big gains quickly—that push-and-pull must be exhausting. Notice how your mind jumps to "it won't be enough"—what if, just for these 15 minutes, we focused on the process (engaging with curiosity) rather than the outcome (how much ground you cover)? Where might you start that feels gently challenging but not overwhelming?

client: I could maybe start by just reviewing the professor's comments on my project for 15 minutes without trying to fix anything. But I'm scared I'll just feel stupid all over again seeing where I went wrong. It's easier to avoid it completely than face that feeling of disappointment in myself.
therapist: It takes real courage to face feedback that's brought up so much self-doubt before—I hear how vulnerable this feels for you. When you imagine reviewing those comments, what would help you stay grounded in remembering this is about improving your work, not measuring your worth?

client: Maybe I could remind myself that even the best students get constructive feedback sometimes. But it's hard because when I see comments on my work, I immediately feel like they're pointing out flaws in me as a person, not just my project. I'm not sure how to separate the two.
therapist: It sounds like you're making an important distinction here—between feedback on your work and judgments about yourself as a person. That automatic jump to personalizing criticism is so common and understandable—what happens if, just during these 15 minutes, you practice noticing when your mind makes that leap and gently guide it back to focusing on the work itself as separate from your self-worth?
